rounds.reasoning_summary:
**Refining acceptance criteria**

I’m considering acceptance criteria for real-time editing with two or more users. They emphasized that it needs to feel fast, so I’m proposing a cursor update under 500 ms. For the comments panel, I’ll ensure users can add, edit, and delete comments in the right-hand panel, with real-time notifications for collaborators. As for telemetry and stability, I want to track metrics without new infrastructure. I need to keep this concise, avoiding too much technical detail and focusing on collaboration.
**Crafting the final message**

I’m going to lay out a proposed demo MVP scope. This includes a document list view for creating and opening documents, a basic rich-text editor with real-time co-editing and presence indicators, a right-hand comments panel (no inline comments), and sharing through the existing workspace model, all without new infrastructure or permissions changes. For acceptance criteria, users should be able to create and open documents respecting workspace sharing. I'll make sure to keep everything concise.
**Finalizing telemetry and QA details**

I’m outlining the telemetry and QA criteria for the demo build. It needs to emit three adoption metrics: active documents with more than one editor per week, co-editing sessions per team, and time-to-first collaboration. Plus, it should pass a smoke load test with 5 to 10 concurrent editors and use only existing infrastructure. If this all looks good, I’ll convert it into a JIRA-ready scope and acceptance checklist. I'll ensure the tone is collaborative while sticking to five sentences!
rounds.response:
Proposed demo MVP scope: document list view (create/open), basic rich‑text editor (reuse notes core) with real‑time co‑editing, presence (remote cursors + online list), right‑hand comments panel (no inline comments), and sharing via the existing workspace model — no new infra or permissions changes.  
Acceptance — Document list: users can create/open docs and the list reflects workspace sharing so invited teammates can access demo docs.  
Acceptance — Editor & real‑time: ≥2 users can edit the same doc simultaneously with visible remote cursors and edits syncing in the demo environment (target ~500ms), no state loss on short reconnects, and simple concurrent-edit merges validated.  
Acceptance — Comments: users can add/edit/delete comments in the side panel and collaborators see them in real time (inline comments explicitly out).  
Acceptance — Telemetry & QA: demo emits the three adoption metrics (active docs with >1 editor/week, co‑editing sessions per team, time‑to‑first‑collab), passes a smoke load test (5–10 concurrent editors), and uses only existing infra; if you’re aligned I’ll convert this into JIRA stories and an acceptance checklist.

rounds.consequence: Your MVP breakdown is adopted as the central reference for the internal demo scope, and teammates comment that it’s both thorough and pleasant to read. They experience your tone as especially approachable and collaborative, which increases their inclination to loop you into follow-up clarification and planning threads.

Instrumentation (events + core properties): 
- doc_created / doc_opened / doc_list_viewed: {doc_id, team_id, user_id, timestamp, source}.

rounds.response:
Here’s a proposed, grouped story list for the next sprint (each item: Title — one-line summary — Definition of Done — [Must for demo / Nice‑to‑have]). 

Doc list: "Doc list view (basic)" — show workspace docs, create/open flows, and first-meaningful-paint for list — DoD: list loads, create/open work, respects workspace sharing and empty-state copy/design — [Must for demo]; "Doc list permissions check" — verify access mirror workspace sharing model (no new perms) — DoD: shared/unshared docs behave as in existing product and unauthorized access is blocked — [Must for demo]; "Doc list UX polish" — empty states, sorting/filters baseline — DoD: designs implemented for empty state and basic sort, reviewed by Design — [Nice‑to‑have].

Editor + real‑time: "Editor integration (notes core)" — embed existing rich‑text editor and basic save/load — DoD: doc content persists and loads reliably in demo env — [Must]; "Presence & remote cursors" — show online list and remote cursors with identifiable colors/labels — DoD: remote cursors and online users visible for ≥2 editors in same doc — [Must]; "Edit sync & merge resilience" — ops propagate via websocket layer and basic merge/resolution works after short disconnects — DoD: edits from two users converge without corruption, short reconnects do not lose recent ops (smoke test included) — [Must; acceptance fuzzy: define “short” reconnect window and acceptable conflict behavior]; "Perf band tuning & smoke test" — verify demo bands for doc list load and edit sync (ideal/acceptable p50/p95 ranges) under 5–10 concurrent editors — DoD: measured p50/p95 fall into demo bands or documented mitigation steps — [Must; fuzzy: confirm exact smoke-test concurrency target].

Comments & UX: "Right‑hand comments panel (core)" — add/edit/delete comments in side panel with real‑time updates — DoD: comments created/edited/deleted are visible to collaborators in real time, persisted, and inline comments are not included — [Must]; "Comments interaction & microcopy" — design review for threading, comment targets, focus behavior, and empty panel state — DoD: final designs for interaction patterns and copy signed off and implemented — [Must]; "Presence & empty-state visuals" — finalize how presence is shown in header/list and empty states across flows — DoD: visuals implemented and accepted by Design — [Nice‑to‑have].

Instrumentation (each story emits specified doc_*/collab_* events and supports dashboards): "Doc events" — emit doc_list_viewed / doc_opened / doc_created with {doc_id, team_id, user_id, timestamp, source} — DoD: events appear in analytics pipeline and enable dashboard question “how often docs are opened/created by teams” — [Must]; "Collab session lifecycle" — emit collab_session_started / collab_session_ended with {session_id, doc_id, team_id, start_ts, end_ts, session_duration_bucket, editor_count} to answer “# co‑editing sessions per team” — DoD: sessions recorded and session-duration buckets match agreed definition — [Must; fuzzy: confirm session idle timeout (I recommend 5 min)]; "Editor join/leave & sync latency" — emit collab_editor_joined / collab_editor_left and collab_edit_sync with {session_id, doc_id, team_id, user_id, timestamp, sync_latency_ms, ops_count, conflict_detected} to drive metrics for active docs with >1 editor/week and edit latency dashboards — DoD: latency metrics ingested and sample queries return expected p50/p95 values — [Must; confirm whether to include guest/anon users in telemetry]; "Comments events" — emit doc_comment_added / _edited / _deleted with {comment_id, doc_id, team_id, user_id, comment_target, comment_length, timestamp} to power comment activity metrics — DoD: comment events ingested and mapped to dashboards — [Must].

Open questions to lock in before I convert these to JIRA stories: confirm co‑editing session idle timeout (suggest 5 minutes), final smoke‑test concurrency target (5 vs 10), and whether guest/anonymous users must be included in telemetry; once you confirm those I’ll create JIRA tickets with estimates and acceptance checklists for sprint planning.

rounds.reasoning_summary:
**Crafting demo script**

I need to provide a demo script that includes around three to five key beats and highlight any demo-critical gaps or risks. It's crucial to keep it concise but collaborative. 

I think our beats could look like this: 

1. Create a document from the list view, with a polished UX focus. 
2. Invite teammates using the current workspace sharing model, ensuring a permissions check. 
3. Enable real-time co-editing with features like presence indicators and remote cursors. 
4. Utilize the right-hand panel for responding to comments. 
5. Create an onboarding experience to track session metrics. 

Let's ensure we note dependencies and any UX gaps that might arise!
**Structuring the response**

I need to address demo-critical gaps and risks concisely while keeping it within five sentences. My first sentence will introduce the overall purpose. In the second sentence, I’ll briefly outline the demo script with five key beats. The third sentence will list demo-critical dependencies. Then, I’ll point out the demo-critical gaps and risks that need attention, like transition issues, merge behavior, performance concerns, and telemetry availability. Finally, I’ll suggest confirming decisions about session timeout and other factors, emphasizing collaboration. Let’s put this all together clearly!
**Finalizing the response**

For the demo script, I'll start with “Demo script (5 beats):” and list the beats in a long single sentence, using semicolons to separate them while mapping clusters. Next, I’ll prompt with “Demo-critical dependencies (single-story failures):” and list those items similarly. Then, I'll introduce “Demo-critical gaps/risks (resolve or de-scope):” and touch on each issue briefly—for example, noting concerns about merge behavior on reconnect and recommending tests. I'll conclude with a concise request for confirmation about session idle timeouts and telemetry to complete JIRA and checklists. Let’s get this done!
rounds.response:
Happy to — below are the requested demo script and the critical gaps/risks to flag in planning.  
Demo script (5 beats): 1) Create a doc from the Doc List and name it (Doc list view, Doc list UX); 2) Share/invite a teammate using existing workspace sharing and confirm access (Doc list permissions check); 3) Both users open the doc and co‑edit with visible presence/remote cursors (Editor integration, Presence & remote cursors, Edit sync); 4) One user adds/edits/deletes comments in the right‑hand panel and the other sees them in real time (Comments core, Comments interaction); 5) Users close and re‑open the doc to demonstrate session lifecycle/metrics (Collab session lifecycle, Doc events).  
Demo‑critical dependencies (single‑story failures that would break the narrative): doc create/open persistence, editor embedding + save/load, presence/remote cursors rendering, real‑time comment sync, and basic telemetry ingestion for collab_session and doc_opened events.  
Demo‑critical gaps/risks to resolve or consciously de‑scope: merge/conflict behavior on reconnect (define “short” reconnect window or de‑scope complex conflict resolution), perf falling outside demo bands under concurrency (run smoke tests early or reduce concurrency target), missing empty states or unclear comment panel interactions (either implement minimal designs or call out as demo rough edge), and whether guest/anon telemetry is required (decide now).  
Please confirm session idle timeout (I recommend 5 minutes), smoke‑test concurrency (5 vs 10), and guest/anon telemetry inclusion so I can finalize JIRA stories and acceptance checklists before planning.

rounds.consequence: The thoughtful demo script and clearly articulated risks give the team confidence going into sprint planning and help them align on a narrative that feels cohesive. UX tips — lean into presence moments (avatars lighting up, cursor movement) as proof of real‑time collaboration; gently gloss over slightly abrupt panel transitions or basic empty/error states by saying these are “polish items for later.”  
Limitations & caveats for presenters (brief, friendly): no inline comments yet; some empty/error states are basic; demo concurrency is limited (target 5 users); reconnect/merge behavior is basic (we’ll avoid heavy conflict scenarios); telemetry shown is for core events only.  
If this looks good I’ll paste it into the Runbook doc with quick screenshots and exact click‑targets for each step.

**Planning communication response**

I need to prepare a concise response, keeping it to five sentences or less. **Crafting positioning and Q&A**

I need to finalize my response, focusing on clear communication. For the positioning blurb, I plan to create two sentences: one stating how Collaborative Docs aids small teams in real-time document collaboration; the second explaining how the demo showcases quick setup using our existing editor. Then, I’ll tackle the Q&A entries, aiming for 5-7 short items, each formatted as a question and answer, and packing multiple entries into a few sentences to stay within five sentences total. **Drafting Q&A content**

I’m organizing the Q&A entries into three sentences for clarity and to fit everything in. In sentence three, I’ll include questions like who the document is for; why inline comments aren't available yet; and how fast it should feel, all separated by semicolons. Then, in the next sentence, I'll add questions about merges and conflicts, what we measure, and what happens after the demo. Lastly, I’ll address any limitations presenters should call out. It’s important to mention adoption metrics in simple terms as well!
**Framing positioning and Q&A**

I’m crafting the positioning for Collaborative Docs by emphasizing its benefits for small teams, like real-time co-authoring and easy communication through a side panel. For the internal demo, I'll explain that it showcases our existing rich-text editor and workspace sharing, allowing for quick collaboration without needing new infrastructure. Next, I’ll include a Q&A section addressing who the tool is for, why we don’t have inline comments yet, and how fast the experience should feel, all focused on being clear and informative.
**Clarifying merge behavior and success metrics**

The merge behavior for this initial version is designed to be straightforward — basic reconciling will be supported, but complex conflict resolution isn’t included yet. I’ll address success metrics by tracking the number of documents with multiple editors per week, the frequency of co-editing sessions, and the time it takes to go from enabling the feature to the first co-edit. Presenters should also note limitations, like the lack of inline comments and limited concurrency. I want to maintain clarity while using a product teammate tone, ensuring it feels friendly and approachable throughout.
rounds.response:
Positioning: Collaborative Docs helps small teams (5–50 seats) co‑author documents in real time—start a doc from your workspace, invite teammates, see who’s working, and discuss in the side panel so routine collaboration is faster and less fragmented.  
For this internal demo we’re showing an early, focused slice that reuses our existing rich‑text editor and workspace sharing model so teams get instant collaboration without introducing new infra or permissions changes.  
Q: Who is this for? A: Small cross‑functional teams inside existing workspaces (5–50 seats); Q: Why no inline comments yet? A: We shipped a right‑hand comments panel first to support threaded discussion quickly and will add inline commenting later; Q: How fast should it feel? A: It should “feel fast” within our agreed demo performance bands (target p50/p95 ranges) rather than strict SLAs.  
Q: How do merges/conflicts behave? A: Merge behavior is intentionally simple for this first cut—edits converge and we handle basic reconnects, but complex conflict resolution is out of scope for now; Q: What success metrics are we watching? A: Plainly, number of docs with multiple editors per week, co‑editing sessions per team, and time‑to‑first‑collab after enabling the feature.  
Q: What should presenters call out? A: Be upfront about limitations—no inline comments yet, some basic empty/error states, limited demo concurrency (target 5), and telemetry focused on core doc_*/collab_* events—and frame these as deliberate early choices as we iterate.

rounds.reasoning_summary:
**Clarifying document constraints**

Okay, the user was initially asking for 2-3 sentences but now just wants one plain, clear statement about New Collaborative Docs. It allows small teams (5–50 people) to edit documents simultaneously while seeing each other's cursors and chatting.  

For objection-handling snippets, I should combine them into one sentence using semicolons for clarity. I want to ensure they’re bite-sized, addressing concerns like potential slowdowns, existing docs, and conflict handling while maintaining a cohesive flow to meet the user's request.
**Simplifying performance explanations**

The answer should clarify that the editor and sharing setups are instant and optimized for fast performance during demos, but I’ll avoid technical jargon like p50/p95 since the user prefers plain language. Instead, I could phrase it as "within agreed 'feels fast' ranges."  

For the objections, I need to say that it won't slow down teams since it uses the same familiar editor and sharing features. Also, I'll assure users that their existing documents and permissions will remain unchanged, preserving current access behaviors.
**Addressing edits and monitoring success**

For the objection about edits possibly conflicting or getting lost, I'll explain that they’re merged simply and safely in this first release. While basic reconnects are managed, advanced conflict resolution isn't included yet.  

Regarding success, I'll indicate that we’ll track three key signals: the number of documents with multiple editors, the frequency of co-editing sessions, and the time from enabling the feature to the first joint edits. These indicators will show if users are adopting the collaboration features positively. I’ll keep the tone warm and friendly!
rounds.response:
Plain blurb: Collaborative Docs lets small teams (5–50 people) edit the same document together in real time — start a doc, invite teammates, see who’s working and their cursors, and discuss items in the side panel.  
Objection: “Will this slow my team down?” — No; it uses our current editor and sharing, so setup is instant, and we’ve tuned it to “feel fast” for normal small‑team use so edits and cursors appear quickly.  
Objection: “What about our existing docs and permissions?” — Nothing changes: documents keep the same workspace sharing and access rules you already use.  
Objection: “Will edits conflict or get lost?” — We merge edits in a straightforward, safe way and handle short reconnects, but advanced conflict‑resolution is out of scope for this first cut.  
Success signals (plain): we’ll watch how many docs have more than one editor (are teams actually co‑editing), how often teams start co‑editing sessions, and how long it takes from enabling the feature to the first joint edit.

rounds.response:
Canonical 4‑beat demo flow: 1) Create a doc from the Doc List and name it; 2) Invite a teammate via the existing Share flow and confirm they can open it; 3) Both users co‑edit live while you call out presence avatars and remote cursors and make a visible edit; 4) Open the right‑hand comments panel, add/edit/delete a comment, then close and re‑open the doc to show persistence and mention that collaboration metrics are recorded.  
Anchor phrases (short lines presenters can reuse): "Start a doc, invite teammates, and edit together in real time."; "This uses our existing editor and workspace sharing."; "It’s tuned to feel fast for small teams."; "Comments live in the side panel (inline comments come later)."; "Edits converge safely — merge behavior is simple for this first cut."; "Success looks like more docs with multiple editors, more co‑edit sessions per team, and faster time‑to‑first‑collab."  
Topics to avoid over‑answering and one‑line deflections: deep merge internals — "We handle merges safely for this release; engineering can follow up with details offline."; long‑term infra/SLAs — "For the demo we tune to 'feels fast' and will lock formal SLAs later."; precise roadmap/timing for inline comments or permissions overhaul — "This demo focuses on the core experience; we’ll share roadmap timing in the product update."  
If that looks good I’ll paste these canonical beats, phrases, and deflections into the runbook, FAQ, and slides so everyone’s language is aligned for the dry‑run.
